title: What are unit economics, and how do you use them in a case?
description: What unit economics means, how to work out the profit on one order, customer or store, and why it is often the fastest way into a case.
hook: "Unit economics" sounds like jargon, but the idea is simple and powerful: before worrying about the whole company, work out whether it makes money on one unit. One order, one customer, one store, one flight. If a single unit loses money, growing faster only loses money faster. Many cases become much clearer the moment you look at one unit.
body:
What counts as a unit?

Whatever the business sells or repeats. For a delivery app it is one order. For a gym it is one member. For a coffee chain it might be one store. For an airline, one flight. Choose the unit that the business decisions are made around.

A worked example: one food delivery order

  • Average order: £25. The app takes a 25% commission: £6.25.
  • Delivery fee paid by the customer: £2.00.
  • Revenue per order: £8.25.
  • Paying the rider: £4.50. Card fees: £0.40. Customer support and refunds: £0.60. Discounts and vouchers: £1.50.
  • Cost per order: £7.00.
  • Contribution per order: £1.25.

Now the big picture questions become easy to frame. With £1.25 per order, the app needs 800,000 orders a month just to cover £1 million of monthly fixed costs like offices and engineers. If vouchers grow, the contribution can quickly turn negative.

Unit economics for customers: LTV and CAC

When the unit is a customer, two numbers matter. LTV (lifetime value) is the profit a customer brings over the whole time they stay. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is what it costs to win them. A healthy business earns comfortably more from each customer than it spent winning them. A common rule of thumb is LTV at least three times CAC.

Why interviewers like it

It shows you can cut through a big, messy problem. Saying "Before looking at the whole company, I'd like to understand the profit on a single order" signals clear thinking, and it often finds the answer quickly.

A phrase to use

Let me first check whether each unit makes money on its own. If it doesn't, growth won't fix the problem.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads.
